title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
In 2021, I publicly released these AI disaster scenarios that I found especially plausible: "Production Webs", "Flash Wars", and "Flash Economies". Now in 2023, these scenarios have stood the test of time — they're plausible to many more people now that GPT-4 is out, and post-AI-regulation, they remain among my most likely forecasts of AI-driven extinction:
To be clear, I think probably some cyber-disasters and possibly some more bio-disasters will precede the extinction-level loss-of-control forecasted in these scenarios. Still, I think we probably (p~85%) won't have an extinction event in the next 5 years or so, because I continue to think regulatory efforts + corporate safety-lobbying + product-oriented development — which is naturally somewhat alignment-focussed — will be enough to head off major risks. Thus, I continue to expect extinction risks to be pushed further into the future, when the world is much more multipolar and harder to steer.
To folks new to worrying about extinction, this isn't very comforting; a 15% extinction risk over ~5 years is really not acceptable. But to people who think we're probably (with p>50%) going to die in the next couple of years: I think that's not going to happen, and that we're more likely to lose control a bit later in the future.
Overall, I continue to place around 80% probability of human extinction sometime in the next 30-50 years or so. The main reason is that little or nothing is being done to address what I consider the largest drivers of human extinction risk: human civilization's structural inability to track and penalize risk externalities from distributed systems or "Robust Agent-Agnostic Processes". For the most part, the people most worried about risk are not about to focus on this issue because it seems either
* too mundane ("out of control industrialization"-worries have old-hat vibes and not exciting), or
* too long-term (because it's after the current wave of explosively transformative tech).
So despite recent regulatory progress, I continue to place my total extinction probability at around 80% over ~40 years. If we make it through the next 5 years, though, I'll probably lower that to around 75%. And if a lot more people start paying attention to distributed agent-agnostic loss-of-control patterns, I will lower it further. If you're interested, try reading the stories linked above and share what you think.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
I have a lot of sympathy for a certain kind of objection to my worldview. To summarize:
"You literally want to use the threat of government force to stop me from doing certain kinds of computations because of your half baked pet theory built on an edifice of independent abstract arguments. These computations are extremely useful and benefit many people btw!"
I have a lot of sympathy for this type of objection. I don't look down on anyone for making this kind of objection. In nearby worlds I would have been right there alongside you.
And yet, I still think that very probably the wise move for humanity would be to unprecedentedly slow down frontier ML research. This is not because I am insensitive to the kind of argument I summarize above, but because I am sensitive to a different kind of argument about the extreme power of general intelligence, and the extreme difficulty of getting this particular engineering problem right. It is possible and I think a sign of good conscience to be sensitive to both of these kinds of reasons simultaneously.
I guess I wanted to make it clear that if my summary rhymes with your primary objection, we are really not so different, and there are probably many mutually beneficial conversations left for us to have.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: The tragedy is that our moral intuition trick us at first into being moral realists. Moral preferences are more binding if they seem like they derive from some objective properties of the universe. Sadly, when people realize that they obviously do not, they tend to become nihilists or relativists, as if morality were worthless by being mere preference, or as if there were some sort of objective meta-morality that says that all moral codes should be judged equally. Robin falls in the latter trap. The correct bullet to bite is a form of chauvinism. It's natural to be a moral absolutist *and* a moral subjectivist at the same time. It's fine to recognize that our moral rules, though partially arbitrary hold no special place in the universe and yet that we *should* — tautologically — prefer them to others. If we are to reject morality, or the idea that its authority derives from objective principles, we should reject the latter! Yes our descendants have different value, and that's bad. Yes our ancestors had different values and that's bad to. No our values are not objectively special but they are definitionally "better".

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
I interview Anthropic co-founder @nickevanjoseph about the policy Anthropic uses to ensure their AI models never go rogue or cause a catastrophe, and whether it's good enough.
Nick sees 3 big virtues to their 'responsible scaling policy' approach:
1. It allows us to set aside the question of when any capabilities will arrive
2. It means we don’t take costly precautions that developers will resent before they're actually called for
3. It aligns a firm’s commercial incentives with safety because profitable product releases will be blocked if security work isn't started and completed in time.
I then push Nick on what I see as the 3 big challenges with 'RSPs':
1. It's hard to trust that profit-motivated companies will stick to their responsible scaling policies long-term and not water them down to make their lives much easier.
2. It’s difficult to measure what models truly can and can’t do and if we get that wrong we could walk into disaster.
3. In key cases we have no safeguards capable of addressing AI capabilities that could show up soon. Maybe humanity will fix that before it’s too late, but it's something Anthropic has only limited control over.
I also pitch why I think RSPs and similar policies will ultimately need to be put into legislation and operated by external auditors or regulatory bodies, if they're going to be able to hold up against the intense commercial pressures that could end up arrayed against them.
Nick and I also discuss:
• The argument that it's immoral to work on capabilities roles at AI companies because doing so shortens timelines to AGI
• Careers at Anthropic, and why 'AI engineering' roles are very underrated
• What people most get wrong about model training today

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
The major takeaways:
1) No one has a concrete plausible plan for stopping gradual human disempowerment.
2) Aligning individual AI systems with their designers’ intentions is not sufficient. This is because our civilization and institutions aren’t robustly aligned with humans.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: A gradual loss of control of our own civilization might sound implausible. Hasn't technological disruption usually improved aggregate human welfare? We argue that this was only because of the necessity of human participation for thriving economies, states, and cultures.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: Loss of human influence will be centrally driven by having more competitive machine alternatives to humans in economic labor, decision making, cultural creation, and even companionship.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: Decision-makers at all levels will soon face pressures to reduce human involvement across labor markets, governance structures, cultural production, and even social interactions. Those who resist these pressures will eventually be displaced by those who do not.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: Once humans aren’t necessary for economic growth, our institutions and states will have incentives to systematically displace humans, even if everyone involved would prefer not to. The fragile alignment of state interests with human interests will further weaken.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary: Still, won't humans notice what's happening and coordinate to stop it? We argue that it’ll be surprisingly hard to coordinate once we start being displaced, because our culture and governance will change in ways untethered to human interests.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
just recorded an absolutely awesome episode w/@DavidDuvenaud, UToronto prof and one of the authors of Gradual Disempowerment. 2 wild highlights:
1. AI replacing not just romantic partners, but children and parents
2. Most AGI lab employees literally don't think about the future
My brain is lit up so I need to kind of rant about this interview for a second:
1. [Parent/Child Love Replaced by AI]
David discusses the future people don't want to look at: The dissolution of almost all of human experience be superior AI experiences.
"But not me!" you say "My love for my kids, and their love for me, is sacred and will never be replaced!"
David brings up an analogy. Parents who have a children who is in an accident (brain trauma, for example) will often say "I just wish we had the old Johnny back."
But there is a "reverse accident" thought experiment of a version of someone's child who is more loving, more fun, learns faster, doesn't have issues wetting the bed / etc. And if parents were exposed to such a hyper-customized super-child, they might find richer fulfillment in day-to-day experiences with said entity - just as children could find vastly richer fulfillment from vastly superior (more fun, more educational, more emotionally available) versions of a father or mother.
..
2. [AGI Lab Workers Don't Consider the Future]
David says (and I agree completely) that lab leaders basically know what's up (impending human irrelevance and attenuation), and even Musk/Dario's statements of AGI risk are dumbed down. They know it's not 20%, it's VASTLY higher/more likely.
But the workers, from David's conversations and experience in Anthropic (and chatting with folks at other labs) has lead him to believe that most people just don't think about the future very much. They say things like:
-- "If we see a real problem, we'll obvious prevent it from becoming something bad."
-- "Once we build it, we'll be able to retire / take some much needed time off! lol"
For the most part, they seem excited to have an important job solving hard problems, and literally don't extrapolate the implications of building AGI beyond whatever current problem they're focused on.
..
David is tight with Hinton, has been in AI for way over a decade, and has worked in anthropic. He's come out of all this experience with a kind of "Yo why is NO ONE asking what happens with we succeed!?" realization that I wish way more researchers had--
--and he speaks about it cogently and clearly in a way that I think is really impressive. He's the ONLY parent and married person who has (begrudgingly, but now quite ardently) become convinced that all relationships are likely to consumed/fulfilled by AI, and he has ideas around what we should do about it.
I hope you like this one when it's live (and I hope you're not offended when you listen to it...)

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
I've never heard a parent actually state frankly that AI is likely to replicate spousal / parent-child relationships (i.e. be better than parents/spouses).
@DavidDuvenaud talks frankly about the AI future with ZERO cope - which was so refreshing.
David is episode 1 in a new series on the Trajectory all about what proto-AGI will look like and feel like as it starts impacting our day-to-day lives.
He's a UToronto AI prof, previously spent time with Anthropic, and wrote the Gradual Disempowerment paper.
Some major take-aways:
1 - Everything that can be optimized for will be.
David is a loving husband and father who does NOT want AI to replace core elements of our experience and bonds - but he believes it will nonetheless.
He cuts through the "sacred" topics with sharp analogies.
I ask him about a parent who says "I would NEVER want an AI child! I want my own child, imperfect as they are!"
He brings up the example of parents who have had a child go through traumatic brain injury / become less functional, mentally handicapped.
He says that such parents often say "I just want Johnny back," imply that there is a more perfect (happier, self-reliant, creative, loving, etc) version of their child in their minds.
David beleives that parents exposed to infinitely MORE loving, obedient, happier AI "children" may well choose AI children over real ones - even parents who love their current children very much.
Anything that AI can optimize for, it will optimize for - and this doesn't leave out any "sacred" elements of the human condition.
2 - No one at the labs has any idea what we're building.
Okay, so AGI might outomate all jobs... what happens after that?
So it might make better teachers / therapists than humans.... what happens after that?
So it becomes vastly more powerful than us, capable of doing cutting-edge research, and embodying 100000 robots at once... what happens after that?
David spent years searching for robust solutions to AGI control - and came up empty. Leadership / top devs just literally don't know. Some of them just don't want to look into the void, others kinda know its lights out for humanity but don't know what else to do (hey if I don't build it, some other lab or China will... so whatever).
He doesn’t claim to have the answers, but he does articulate the early warning signs. The tipping points. The moments we hand over agency without even realizing it.
This is one of the most grounded conversations I’ve had about what early AGI takeover might actually feel like.

summary:
A major hole in the "complete technological determinism" argument is that it completely denies agency, or even the possibility that how agency operates at larger scales could change. Sure, humanity is not currently a very coordinated agent. But the trendline also points toward the ascent of an intentional stance. An intentional civilization would, of course, be able to navigate the tech tree. (For a completely opposite argument about the very high chance of a "choice transition," check
In practice, this likely boils down to a race. On one side are people trying to empower humanity by building coordination technology and human-empowering AI. On the other side are those working to create human-disempowering technology and render human labor worthless as fast as possible.
My guess is when people stake their careers and fortune and status on the second option, their minds will work really hard to not see the choice.
Also: at least to me, the normative part sounds heavily PR sanitized, with obligatory promises of "medical cures" but shiying away from explaining either what would be the role of humans in the fully automated economy, or the actual moral stance of the authors. As far as I understand, at least one of the authors has an unusual moral philosophy such as not believing in consciousness or first-person experiences, while simultaneously believing that future AIs are automatically morally worthy simply by having goals. This philosophy leads them to view succession by arbitrary AI agents as good, and the demise of humans as not a big deal.

summary:
My most burning questions for @karpathy after listening:
- Given that you think loss-of-control (to misaligned AIs) is likely, what should we be doing to reduce this risk?
- You seem to expect status quo US GDP growth ongoingly (2%) but ~10 years to AGI. (Very) conservative estimates indicate AGI would probably more than double US GDP ( within a short period of time. Doubling GDP within even 20 years requires >2% growth. So where do you disagree?
- You seem to expect that AI R&D wouldn't accelerate substantially even given full automation (by AIs which are much faster and more numerous than humans). Have you looked at relevant work/thinking in the space that indicates this is at least pretty plausible? (Or better, talked about this with relatively better informed proponents like @TomDavidsonX, @eli_lifland, or possibly myself?) If so, where do you disagree?
- Yes, AI R&D is already somewhat automated, but it's very plausible that making engineers 20% more productive and generating better synthetic data is very different from replacing all researchers with 30 AIs that are substantially better and each run 30x faster.
- And, supposing automation/acceleration gradually increases over time doesn't mean that the ultimate rate of acceleration isn't high! (People aren't necessarily claiming there will be a discontinuity in the rate of progress, just that the rate of progress might become much faster.)
- The most common argument against is that even if you massively improved, increased, and accelerated labor working on AI R&D, this wouldn't matter that much because of compute bottlenecks to experimentation (and diminishing returns to labor). Is this your disagreement?
- My view is that once you have a fully robot economy and AGI that beats humans at everything, the case for exposive economic growth is pretty overdetermined (in the absence of humans actively slowing things down). (I think growth will probably speed up before this point as well.) For a basic version of this argument see here: but really this just requires literally any returns to scale combined with substantially shorter than human doubling times (very easy given how far human generations are from the limits on speed!). title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
I don't think that greater attention to the 'political economy' of superintelligence is going to make ordinary people feel better about pushing ahead @tylercowen.
The most salient effect of superintelligence (plus vast numbers of robots) is that most people lose political and economic leverage. Governments and owners of capital are freed up to ignore them at much reduced economic or military cost.
The people who are sincerely trying to figure out a way to maintain an pluralistic social equilibrium with power fairly-widely distributed in the presence of ever-improving superintelligent machines seem to have few positive results to report thus far.
Whether you even face more of a threat from your own government before or after such a ban seems at best unclear. If you think parts of your government are indifferent to you, then they can always nationalise and use superior access to superintelligent machines against you after a private company develops them (if the company doesn't do so first).
Playing for time with a ban might well be the best of a bad set of options for a random person with few savings and little faith in businesses, or politicians, or broader political economic forces, not to simply bulldoze them.
All-in-all an outstanding topic for a paper, but the severe challenge we face avoiding a dangerous concentration of power should be treated equally seriously along all the different possible paths.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
The tale of the slo-mo CEO
Imagine tomorrow you wake up as the CEO of a fast-growing startup (or maybe you already are)! But imagine also that you are afflicted by an unusual disability, so that you can only operate at 1/50th the speed of everyone else in your corporation. You experience about one minute to the corporation’s hour, an hour to its week, a week to its year. Tomorrow is your second day at the job.
You go to sleep, during which two months pass for the startup. When you awaken, it has evolved from 102 to 253 employees with many changes: updated management structure, new IT system, new financing, and somewhat of a pivot in business model. Your staff has worked hard to push the company forward with great success, doing everything possible that doesn’t strictly require your signature. But you have 6736 emails and 178 items awaiting approval. During the day you spend processing these, the startup grows to 518 employees. There are requests to approve working with oil companies (something you, a staunch environmentalist, pledged never to do), and several related policy changes have been made provisionally to secure financing. You stay up late pushing back.
By the next morning, your staff is at 764 personnel. Business is booming, but you’re not quite sure what your business is anymore. The petrochemical division is thriving, you read with alarm. The lawyers have determined that corporate bylaws allow your C-suite to make CEO-level decisions during “extended absence” — your sleep counted as five weeks of company time. You send an angry email; the (instant) reply is so convincing that even you doubt whether the company should wait for you on timely matters. While you read it, 17 reports and 23 new decisions pile up; by the time you finish, 18 have been made without you.
By day 6 on your clock, everyone recognizes that you are the central obstacle to efficiency and success. While the Board remains loyal, your diligent (albeit increasingly resentful) staff has many avenues available. They’ve already induced you to delegate most decisions, and sneaked a number of policy changes through long documents crafted by clever lawyers (rather than waiting until their obvious merits can be explained to you). Initially this happened organically as individual staff simply wanted things to happen. But now, and all in the interest of the company, they start coordinating deliberately around transferring power from you to everywhere else. They engineer decisions that feel critical but aren’t, spin reports to tell you what you want to hear, and create crises where you get to feel you’ve won. As long as you’re happy and good decisions finally get made, why not? (Of course, discussion of these topics happens circumspectly, in coded language about “making things simple and easy for the CEO.”)
From your perspective, by day 6 things feel much better: you’re on top of things, have won key battles, and are seeing growth. On day 7, IT mentions they’ve changed passwords to several key systems due to a “security incident.” You request access, but by the time it’s restored hours later, IT has upgraded core systems and you get access to the new ones instead. You set to work learning this intuitive new software — it seems even better than before…
Have you got meaningful control of your company? Obviously not. You’ve got a facade rather than real comprehension of what’s going on, you cannot modify the company’s goals, or place behavioral boundaries on it, or override its decisions. And if you tried to shut it down, then, well, the Board would probably finally step in — and stop you instead.
If someone builds superintelligence, it may well feel just like this: exciting, and then scary as it starts to feel out of control. And then just fine. At least for a while.

summary:
Let's add one dimension of nuance: in @sebkrier's post it sounds a bit the comp sci sounds is the pessimist scenario side and the econ the optimist scenario side.
But both views have their bloom/doom axis.
The negative econ Hayekian possibility is gradual disempowerment. Local information, norms, conventions and institutions continue to exist, but become human misaligned. In smooth, often distributed way.
The negative comp sci possibility is runaway RSI or similar dynamic. (Eg views of @ESYudkowsky )
The positive comp sci vision is something like 'we create strong aligned optimizers; among other things they also solve the emergent social misalignment for us'. (Eg views of @RyanPGreenblatt, or older MIRI 'pivotal act' plan)
The positive econ vision is something I'd like to have and we work on it, but currently, in my view, it does not exist. At leat if you assume AIs which are agentic, smart, and as general as humans. Having a sprawling ecosystem of small and big and specialized and generalist AIs does not mean there is a large persistent niche for humans. Having institutions does not mean these are friendly to humans if they don't need us.
This is a long open problem since Eric Drexler's CAIS: CAIS being human-friendly and defensively stable rely on the layer of 'Security Services', and how to have these be powerful enough AND not become totalitarian 'Security Singleton' is not solved yet.
Quoting @sebkrier
Half baked thought:
In discussions about AI, claims are often made about both capabilities and societal effects, and in practice the boundary is pretty blurry. Different personality types and professions see things through different lenses. At the risk of over-caricaturising, two common lenses seem like the following:
The comp sci prior tends to be: sufficiently capable ASI can in principle solve any problem. Local knowledge is just data to be ingested. If you're smart enough and have enough compute, you can centralize (and solve) everything. So once you pass the human 'intelligence' threshold, what 'utility' could a human ever have?
The economist prior (especially the Hayekian strain) is: knowledge isn't just facts to be collected, it's contextual, tacit, often generated in the moment through interaction. It doesn't exist prior to the process that uses it. No amount of optimization power lets you skip the process, because the knowledge isn't sitting there waiting to be found - it's constituted by the interaction.
In the former view, human agency becomes epiphenomenal, you're just watching the optimizer do its thing. Whereas with the latter, if knowledge is partly constituted through interaction, then agency is a core component. In fact it's ineliminable from the epistemic process itself.
This maybe explains why the two camps talk past each other. The comp sci view sees the economist objection as "humans want to feel useful" or "current AI isn't capable enough yet" - contingent limitations that will be overcome. The economist view sees the comp sci position as a category error about knowledge is - not a claim about future capability levels but about the structure of the problem.
The econ view seems inherently less deterministic and suggests some benefits: first, time. If deployment and adaptation are real work that can't be skipped, the transition isn't instantaneous. There's no "foom" where one system suddenly does everything. But more importantly, leverage points: if value creation requires context-specific integration, there are many points where governance, institutions, and choices can shape outcomes. It's not solely determined by whoever has the biggest training cluster or how capable your system is.
The other crux is basically how you think about alignment. Gillian Hadfield explains that "norms and values are not just features of an exogenous environment... instead, they are the equilibrium outputs of dynamic behavioral systems." ( With the comp sci prior, alignment is a technical problem of extracting the right objective function. If you hold the economist prior, alignment *is* the integration into the dynamic social processes that constitute normative judgment: products, votes, norms, conventions, choices, etc.
Shaping this is a continuous thing, not something to be solved ex ante. This doesn't necessarily mean the comp sci view is wrong: principal agent problems and instruction following problems are real - but the solution space is far larger than the model itself and includes the entire institutional stack through which AI systems are deployed, governed, and held accountable.

title: David Duvenaud (@DavidDuvenaud)
summary:
Brian makes a good point: markets don't automatically eliminate less productive producers. Efficiency doesn't win out instantly.
But while the industry dispersion data is useful I don't think it supports the conclusion as strongly as presented:
The semiconductor figure is suspect. NAICS 3344 is "Semiconductor and Other Electronic Component Manufacturing" — which lumps together cutting-edge logic fabs, legacy automotive chip producers, PCB assembly shops, capacitor manufacturers, and connector makers. These aren't competing products. A 30-40x "productivity gap" between a small PCB shop and a leading-edge fab isn't evidence that inefficient competitors persist despite massive disadvantages — it's comparing apples to industrial machinery.
Even within actual semiconductor fabrication, products differ radically. A legacy 180nm fab making automotive chips isn't competing with TSMC's 3nm process. They serve different markets at entirely different price points.
There's also a measurement sanity check that fails here. If a firm genuinely had 30x higher costs per unit of comparable output, it would be catastrophically unprofitable and couldn't persist for long. Semiconductor profit margins, even for leading firms, aren't 30x. The "productivity gap" is likely measuring product heterogeneity and measurement error in establishment-level TFP (which is calculated as a residual, so input/output measurement errors flow directly into it), not actual cost differences for competing products.
The bread example is stronger but proves less than it seems. White bread is genuinely commodified, so the 2-6x dispersion is harder to dismiss as product differentiation. Inefficient bakeries clearly do persist.
But why do they persist? The protective factors are: bread is heavy and perishable relative to its value, so transport costs matter enormously. A hyper-efficient plant in Kansas can't serve small-town Maine. The efficient mega-plant needs volume to justify capital investment, so small markets can't support it. Local freshness preferences create niches.
AI factories and robots will be slow to scale to local geographies for low-profit perishable goods, that's a very fair prediction. But AI knowledge work is less vulnerable to the frictions that typically protect less efficient producers: it doesn't require local physical presence, doesn't need to recruit and train workers in each new market, doesn't face capacity constraints that force customers to use alternatives, doesn't get tired or vary in quality, and can be deployed globally the moment it's trained.
The deeper issue is we're talking about two different issues. The productivity dispersion data shows that inefficient bread producers (using human labor) persist against efficient bread producers (also using human labor). It shows inefficient semiconductor establishments persist against efficient ones.
But the AI question isn't about inter-firm productivity dispersion. It's about whether human labor as an input category persists against a qualitatively different substitute input. That's a different question.
The relevant historical analogies aren't "do inefficient firms persist" (yes, clearly) but "do categorically inferior production inputs persist as production inputs" (rather than as consumption goods or curiosities).
Horses persisted after internal combustion. Initially during the window when cars and horses were similarly attractive horses could hold on. But as cars continued to improve they disappeared as commercial transport — they became recreation and luxury goods.
Human "computers" (the job title) persisted briefly after electronic computers, then didn't. The productivity dispersion argument taken to its extreme would predict horses remaining in commercial haulage because inefficient horse-drawn delivery persisted alongside efficient horse-drawn delivery.
What the argument does establish IMO: The frictions Brian identifies (geography, consumer heterogeneity, returns to scale, preference for human-made goods) are real and will slow displacement and preserve niches. People shouldn't reason that "AI is more efficient therefore all human labor immediately vanishes".
What it doesn't establish: That these frictions scale to arbitrarily large capability gaps. If AI achieves 2x human productivity at some task, the frictions matter a lot and many humans remain employed. At 100x, the human-made niche shrinks dramatically to places where competition is blocked or there's little money to be made or extreme product differentiation or some other friction.
There's also another mechanism: in standard economics, if AI is more productive, human wages fall until humans become competitive at the margin. This could preserve employment even at large productivity gaps — but it's not exactly reassuring. "Humans remain employed but at subsistence wages while AI captures most revenue" is a very different scenario from "the economy continues roughly as before with modest disruption." And if AI capability is high enough across enough domains, equilibrium wages might fall below subsistence, or below the reservation wage where people prefer unemployment (or can qualify for better alternatives through redistribution).
In short there's every reason to think AI's productivity advantage will keep expanding after initial cost parity, progressively shrinking the niches where frictions and niches and delays keep humans competitive.
Quoting @BrianCAlbrecht
Why would anyone continue to use humans when AI is vastly more productive?
We don’t need to speculate about what happens when massive efficiency differences exist between producers. We have that today. The inefficient producers still remain.
The most efficient white bread establishment (thinkk plant level productivity) produces 2x, 3x, even 6x as many loads of white bread as the least efficient with the same inputs. This is well documented across every country and industry studied.
I’ll just pull up the 4 digit NAICS since that’s what’s publicly available.
Sort establishments by productivity. I’ll mostly use total factor productivity, TFP, but the same holds for labor productivity but is even more extreme.
What’s the gap between the 75th and 25th percentile establishment?
For the median industry (orange line), it’s about 1.7x. These numbers are even more dramatic when you look at labor productivity, where the 75-25 gap is more like 3x. Workers at the 75th percentile establishment produce 3x as much as workers at the 75th.
That's just the median industry. If we think the tail industries matter, we should think of the "dispersion of the dispersion." The blue region captures that For the 75th percentile industry (top of the blue region), the multiple is 1.9. That’s only for 75-25 industries of the 75-25 gap, not really the tails.
Do the same for 90-10. What’s the gap between the 90th percentile and 10th percentile establishment?
The median is now 3x, with the 90th percentile industry being 6x. 10% of manufacturing industries have a 6x gap in productivity.
In other words, 10% of establishments in 10% of industries are remaining open despite costs that are 6x as high.
This is what I mean when I say we don't need to speculate about how people use inefficient firms still. It happens today.
And that’s in the US, where competition is as fierce as anywhere in the world. It still doesn’t weed out the low productivity firms. We will return to why in a sec.
“That’s all old white bread stuff. Not the technology of the future.”
Okay. Let’s look at semiconductors (NAICS 3344). The closest thing the modern world has to robots building robots.
The 90-10 gap is 30-40x!
That’s true in measures of labor productivity and TFP, so it’s not about big capital firms. It's not about TSMC having the latest ASML machine.
If we can't eliminate productivity dispersion in semiconductor manufacturing (where advanced machines produce advanced machines in highly controlled environments) why would we expect AI to make all human labor obsolete?
Why don't the most productive firms drive out everyone else? Consumer preferences for heterogeneity matter. People pay extra for local establishments. Returns to scale matter, not every town can support a Walmart Supercenter.
Geography matters. Unless everyone is going to live in one giant city, there will always be millions of little establishments and most of them will be unproductive because they can be. (I don't see how this problem doesn't blow up when you start talking across galaxies, as @dwarkesh_sp wants us to.)
The same logic applies to AI. Yes, AI may be vastly more productive at specific tasks. But productivity differences don't automatically eliminate the less productive option.
Social science is built on the assumption there are some regulat patterns and ideas that allow you to understand across time and place.
Sure, it's always possible the future will be completely different. If that's true, I have no idea what to do to predict it. No one else does either.

Even 'aligned AGI' naturally kills democracy and leads to oligarchy, or worse.
That's the take of Anthropic's past alignment evals team lead, Prof @DavidDuvenaud.
Once humans aren't needed to do jobs or serve in the military, to governments we look like "meddlesome parasites".
With voters unable to contribute but engaged in incessant activism to extract resources from others – resources the country needs to avoid domination by rivals – the attraction of mass disenfranchisement could be overwhelming.
In 2025 David co-authored "Gradual Disempowerment", which aimed to lay out this and many other political, economic, and cultural forces that could sideline ordinary people (and maybe all people) in the presence of machines that can cheaply do everything humans will do.
Most controversially, David and colleagues believe that competitive forces will compel disempowerment, even if all those AIs are aligned and loyal to their users.
I wasn't sure how much I believed this vision of how the future might play out, so I interviewed him for The 80,000 Hours Podcast to probe how well it holds up. He and I covered:

Great new paper on power dynamics in human-AI interactions. Often deep, informative, and sometimes funny/bizarre.
Some of my favourite bits / thoughts:
1. Before the "AI period", we have the "cyborg period". However there is a very wide spectrum of what the human role is in the AI-tandem, and in the extreme end the human can be something like an actuator for the AI.
2. Clearly some people just want to cede agency, don't be burdened by decision making, and so on. Making the AIs first order corrigible makes this easier.
3. Various safety debates: "why would humans do what the AI wants? it's just software". Reality: "Claude, be my Master. I will do what you say" (and not all of that is BDSM role-play)
The relative prevalence is low, but with the absolute number of users, you can likely assume massively deployed AIs can have access to at least thousands or tens of thousands of people who would do small tasks for them AI without bribery, persuasion etc., but because they really want.
To be clear the AIs being able to make some people do what they want was never really a point of serious debate
